works.title: Baopuzi neipian (Inner Chapters of the Master Who Embraces Simplicity)
works.dateText: substantially complete c. 317 CE, revised to c. 330
works.author: Ge Hong 葛洪 (283–343)
works.structure: 20 Inner Chapters. Chapter list verified this round: 1 Changxuan, 2 Lunxian, 3 Duisu, 4 Jindan (Gold and Cinnabar), 5 Zhili, 6 Weizhi, 7 Sainan, 8 Shizhi, 9 Daoyi, 10 Mingben, 11 Xianyao (Medicines of Immortality), 12 Bianwen, 13 Jiyan, 14 Qinqiu, 15 Zaying, 16 Huangbai (Yellow and White), 17 Dengshe (Climbing and Crossing), 18 Dizhen, 19 Xialan (Broad Overview — a CATALOGUE of Daoist books and talismans, not their contents), 20 Quhuo.

procedures.subject: waidan — laboratory compounding of mineral elixirs, chiefly the cyclically reverted cinnabar elixir and 'potable gold', chapters 4 and 16
procedures.structureOfProcedure: Ge Hong names elixir METHODS and cites the Taiqing (Great Clarity) source scriptures by title; the operative shape is a repeated cyclical refinement in a sealed and luted vessel, the product taken internally. Ingredient identities are named in the text; this record does not reproduce quantities, firing schedules, or vessel preparation.
procedures.completenessEvidence: Ge Hong describes the methods at the level of naming and endorsing them and refers the reader onward to the Taiqing scriptures he lists in ch. 19 (Xialan), which is a bibliography rather than a set of recipes; Pregadio's Great Clarity (2006) treats the Baopuzi as the fullest EARLY SOURCE ON the Taiqing corpus rather than as that corpus itself. Ge Hong further states his own transmission came under oath from his master Zheng Yin and that essentials pass by oral instruction — so what is withheld is exactly the executable layer. MISSING: the source-scripture recipe texts (only some of which survive), the oral keys, and the apparatus detail.

harm.note: The elixir ingredients named include mercury and mercury sulfide, arsenic compounds, and lead compounds — all documented poisons. Historical ingestion of elixirs on this doctrine is documented to have killed practitioners and Tang emperors (Ho Ping-Yü & Needham; the repo already carries this as an atlas edge from baopuzi). Recorded here as the history of a claim, never as a preparation.

procedures.subject: protective fu (talismans) for mountain entry and demon-avoidance, chapter 17 (Dengshe), with talisman titles catalogued in chapter 19
procedures.structureOfProcedure: Ch. 17 concerns the hazards of entering mountains and the apotropaic apparatus — talismans, mirrors, timing and day-selection — held to make passage safe; ch. 19 registers talismans by name.
procedures.completenessEvidence: The chapter names and endorses talismans and lists them by title but the operative content of a fu is its GRAPH, and ch. 19 is explicitly a catalogue. Whether the received Daozang recension of ch. 17 carries reproduced talisman graphs was NOT verified this round (unverified). Graded 'referenced' on the conservative reading.
procedures.vocabGap: talisman-drawing / celestial-script inscription is not the same act as consecration-of-object; the vocabulary has no term for the drawing.
procedures.citation: Wikipedia 'Baopuzi' chapter list (tertiary, this round); Pregadio 2006 for the Taiqing talisman context

procedures.subject: preliminary regimen — retreat to mountains, abstinences, dietary and behavioural preconditions before elixir work
procedures.completenessEvidence: Preconditions are asserted as necessary across chs. 4, 11 and 17 but are nowhere set out as an ordered regimen with durations; the text treats them as known to a properly transmitted disciple.

harm.note: Grain-avoidance and related dietary regimens are described in the tradition as preparatory; recorded as history, with no nutritional claim.

works.title: Zhouyi cantong qi (Seal of the Unity of the Three)
works.dateText: accretional; traditionally attributed to Wei Boyang, 2nd c. CE; received text later (dating contested)
works.author: attributed to Wei Boyang 魏伯陽; in fact anonymous/accretional
works.structure: Emblematic verse. Pregadio's analysis: the work 'seals into one' three subjects — Yijing trigram/hexagram emblems, Daoist (Daodejing/Huang-Lao) cosmology, and alchemy. The atlas already records that Kan and Li stand for the ingredients and that lunar-cycle hexagram sequences govern the 'fire phases'.

procedures.subject: elixir work encoded in trigram and lunar-cycle emblems ('fire phases')
procedures.structureOfProcedure: The text supplies an EMBLEMATIC GRAMMAR — a correspondence system between Yijing figures, the lunar cycle, and the stages of a refining process — rather than an operational sequence.
procedures.completenessEvidence: There is no ingredient list with quantities, no apparatus description, and no ordered step sequence; the correspondences are stated as cosmological analogy. This is why the entire later commentarial tradition (waidan and neidan alike) had to supply the operative reading, and why the same verses were read both ways. Pregadio 2011 treats it as a 'seal' of three subjects, not a recipe.

harm.note: Read as waidan, the emblems 'true lead' and 'true mercury' point at actual lead and mercury compounds — documented severe poisons. The atlas entry already carries this note. Described for study only.

procedures.citation: Pregadio, The Seal of the Unity of the Three (Golden Elixir Press, 2011)

procedures.subject: the same emblems read as neidan — timing of inner 'fire phases' mapped onto breath and inner essences
procedures.completenessEvidence: This reading is supplied by the commentators (from the Tang–Song neidan tradition onward), not by the base text; the base text does not name a breath sequence at all.

works.title: Huangting jing (Scripture of the Yellow Court), Inner and Outer versions
works.dateText: Outer version most likely 2nd-c. Eastern Han; Inner version a Shangqing-linked expansion roughly a century later (3rd–4th c.) — the atlas already flags the Inner/Outer priority as contested
works.author: anonymous / revealed by 'senior deities' in the text's own frame
works.structure: Two related scriptures, both in lines of seven characters, meant to be chanted. Tao Hongjing (456–536) compiled and commented on it (web-verified this round).

procedures.subject: body-god visualization (cunsi) — the indwelling deities of the five viscera and the body's 'palaces' and 'chambers'
procedures.structureOfProcedure: The verse functions as an INVENTORY: it names the inner deities, their offices in a bureaucratic hierarchy, their palaces, and their colour-and-five-phase attributes. The stated aim is to keep the gods in place and prevent their departure. It is a catalogue of what is to be held in mind, not a sitting protocol.
procedures.completenessEvidence: MISSING: posture, sequence, duration, session structure, and the order in which the deities are taken up — none of which the verse supplies. The operative sequencing comes from outside the text: Tao Hongjing's 5th-c. commentary is described as 'clarifying the text's meditative instructions', which is itself evidence that the base text does not stand alone. Graded partial, not referenced, because the WHAT of the visualization (the full deity roster and its attributes) is genuinely given.
procedures.vocabGap: no type for 'chanted scripture doubling as a visualization checklist'.
procedures.citation: Huang & Kohn, 'Internal Gods in Chinese Visual Culture'; Kohn (ed.), The Yellow Court Scripture vols. 1–3 (Three Pines Press/UH Press, 2023–2025)

procedures.subject: chanted recitation of the scripture itself
procedures.completenessEvidence: The seven-character metre and the tradition's use of the text as a chanted scripture are documented, but the text does not itself state repetition counts, occasions, or a recitation liturgy.
procedures.vocabGap: scriptural chanting at prescribed counts is not the same act as mantra-recitation.

procedures.completenessEvidence: Named as the mechanism ('concentrating energy and refining essence') without any ordered breath sequence.

works.title: Shangqing dadong zhenjing (Perfect Scripture of the Great Cavern of Highest Clarity)
works.dateText: core material from the Shangqing revelations of 364–370 CE; received recensions later and divergent
works.author: anonymous; some attribute it to the medium Yang Xi (330–c. 386), presented as celestial dictation
works.structure: Thirty-nine chapters/sections. The first volume, 'Recitation of Scriptures and Jade Formulae', frames the practice; volumes 2–6 carry the main scriptural content. Chen Jingyuan's Song commentary ('Meanings of the Jade Formulae') is the principal exegesis. Catalogued in the Dongzhen (Pervasive Perfection) division of the Zhengtong Daozang.

procedures.subject: cunsi — visualizing indwelling and descending deities, and the pneumas of the five directions, the sun, the moon, and the twenty-four constellations
procedures.structureOfProcedure: Section-by-section: each of the thirty-nine chapters attaches a visualization and an accompanying formula, with the practitioner visualizing a spirit's descent to a position in the body.
procedures.completenessEvidence: The scripture prescribes WHAT is visualized and recited section by section, but the operative keys are the separately transmitted 'jade formulae' (yujue) and oral instructions, which is precisely why Chen Jingyuan's commentary exists to supply them; and the daoinfo/FYSK entry states that 'there have been different versions from the beginning', so no single received sequence is authoritative. MISSING: the transmission-restricted keys and a stable text.
procedures.citation: Isabelle Robinet, Taoist Meditation: The Mao-shan Tradition of Great Purity (SUNY, 1993); en.daoinfo.org FYSK entry (tertiary, this round)

procedures.subject: silent recitation of incantations paired with each section
procedures.completenessEvidence: The pairing of recitation with visualization is structural and documented; the formulae themselves are transmission-restricted and are not reproduced here.

procedures.subject: talismans (fu) accompanying the scripture
procedures.completenessEvidence: Talismans are described as part of the scripture's apparatus but the graph forms and their consecration are not set out in accessible scholarship consulted this round.

procedures.subject: ordination/transmission required before the scripture may be used
procedures.completenessEvidence: Shangqing practice is transmission-gated in Robinet's account; the gate is named, the rite is not set out in this scripture.

works.title: Zhen'gao (Declarations of the Perfected)
works.dateText: compiled c. 499 CE from autograph materials of 364–370
works.author: Tao Hongjing 陶弘景 (456–536), compiler and annotator; underlying material from the medium Yang Xi and the Xu family

Graded fragmentary rather than partial for that reason.

works.title: Wuzhen pian (Awakening to Reality)
works.author: Zhang Boduan 張伯端 (c. 987–1082; Crowe gives c. 983–1081)
works.structure: A cycle of poems in fixed forms — the core that Pregadio translates is the set of sixteen 'regulated verses' (lüshi); the full received text adds quatrains and song-lyrics (the usual tallies of 16 lüshi + 64 jueju + 1 lüshi + 12 ci are NOT re-derived this round — unverified). Written to be chanted.

procedures.subject: neidan — symbolic-physiological inner alchemy: gathering the emblems 'true lead' and 'true mercury' and refining essence, breath and spirit in the 'tripod' of the body
procedures.structureOfProcedure: The poems present the work as a sequence of emblematic operations governed by 'fire phases' inherited from the Cantong qi. The physiology is symbolic; the atlas entry already records that no physical elixir is compounded and that the text itself warns against ingesting minerals.
procedures.completenessEvidence: THIS IS THE SLICE'S CLEANEST CASE OF DELIBERATE INCOMPLETENESS. The verses are allusive poetry, not procedure: no posture, no session structure, no duration, no criterion of success. The tradition's own position is that the essentials pass by oral instruction (koujue) from a master, and the evidence for that is the commentarial apparatus the text immediately grew — Weng Baoguang's Wuzhen zhizhi xiangshuo sansheng biyao ('Straightforward Directions … and the Secret Essentials') and, six centuries later, Liu Yiming's Wuzhen zhizhi ('Straightforward Directions') — both of which are titled as though supplying what the base text withholds, and both of which remain symbolic themselves. Graded 'referenced', NOT 'partial': the text names its operations without setting any of them out.

harm.note: Two distinct hazards. (a) Neidan 'fire phases' have historically been read as breath-retention regimens; breath retention carries hypoxia risk. (b) The far commoner historical harm is the reverse misreading — taking the emblems 'lead' and 'mercury' literally, which the Wuzhen pian itself rejects as a 'side gate' and which the waidan record shows to have been lethal. Recorded as history, not guidance.

procedures.citation: Fabrizio Pregadio, Awakening to Reality (Golden Elixir Press, 2009); Pregadio, Taoist Internal Alchemy: An Anthology of Neidan Texts; Paul Crowe, 'Chapters on Awakening to the Real', B.C. Asian Review 12 (2000)

procedures.subject: the timed 'fire phases' read onto breath and inner essences
procedures.completenessEvidence: Named in emblematic terms only; the timing schema is astronomical-emblematic (lunar-cycle hexagram sequences borrowed from the Cantong qi), not a stated respiratory practice.

works.structure: A method-plus-casebook text: it derives hexagrams from numbers taken from the time and circumstances of the question rather than from a randomizer (stalks, coins, dice), then reads the result through a ti/yong (host/guest) analysis. procedures.subject: number-derived hexagram casting and ti/yong interpretation
procedures.structureOfProcedure: Recorded as a method KIND only: hexagram derivation from circumstantial numbers, then a relational reading between the two trigrams. No derivation rules are reproduced.
procedures.completenessEvidence: Complete AS RECEIVED — the text sets out a method that can be followed end to end, which is why it circulates as a practical manual today. edges.evidence: THE SLICE'S KEY CROSS-CULTURAL EDGE AND THE ONE THE REPO'S OWN PLAN ASKED FOR. Kūkai brought a copy of the Xiuyao jing to Japan on his return in 806; the Heian divinatory school called Sukuyōdō is named after and based on the Xiuyao jing, and it competed with the older, Chinese-derived Onmyōdō. The Japanese recension family of the text is traced back to Kūkai's import. Kūkai is described as the first to press for its introduction and as answering questions about its implementation.
